extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, paleontologists, and graduate students studying disciplinary formation and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the criteria and standards proposed for making paleontology (or a scientific specialty) an autonomous discipline: what problems, resources, methods, and kinds of laws are required. Focuses on Gould/Newell-era strategies (modeling, lawmaking, and proprietary phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation from other disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: The survival of paleontology as an independent discipline depends on whether it could successfully isolate itself from the disciplinary trajectories of both geology and biology; paleontology’s autonomy required that it was able to do more than take its direction from the scientific demands of these other disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation lessens the degree to which paleontological practices contribute to goals that matter equally or more to practitioners outside paleontology; increasing isolation is central to fulfilling the 'intrinsicality' condition for a Darwinian population of practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of a defensible resource
rubrics_metrics.description: "Control of some defensible resource" — identify and monopolize a set of scientific problems that paleontologists alone are uniquely equipped to metabolize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolization of a resource provides proprietary access to important problems and is essential for disciplinary autonomy; examples include phenomena like mass extinction or uniquely paleontological fossil patterns that outsiders cannot authenticate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsicality condition for Darwinian populations
rubrics_metrics.description: A Darwinian population of scientific practices requires (1) increasing isolation from other populations and (2) monopolization of some resource so that differences in practice success relate to goals important to insiders but not outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both components are essential because they make it possible for the success of practices to be driven by criteria internal to the nascent discipline rather than external disciplinary demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify unique, significant problems accessible only to the discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Find fossil phenomena of unambiguous evolutionary importance yet resistant to existing (e.g., Darwinian gradualist) explanations so the discipline can formulate laws accounting for those phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simpson’s 'quantum evolution' and Newell/Cloud’s focus on mass extinction and eruptive evolution are historical examples: the discipline must propose phenomena that provide proprietary explanatory opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish methodological vs substantive uniformitarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological uniformitarianism (assumption that laws of nature remain constant across time and space) is a general scientific procedural warrant, whereas substantive uniformitarianism (that rates of geological change are constant) is an empirical claim that may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain methodological uniformitarianism as a warrant for inductive projection to unobserved cases; do not conflate it with substantive claims about constant rates, because the latter can undermine a discipline’s ability to recognize novel phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use nomic spatiotemporal invariance to project from observed to unobserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Science (including geology/paleontology) relies on the assumption that the laws of nature are spatiotemporally invariant to justify extrapolation from finite observations to unexamined cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basis for treating geology/paleontology as empirical sciences; it legitimates using present knowledge to infer past (unobserved) states.

rubrics_metrics.name: When known laws fail, search for new laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If fossil phenomena resist subsumption under known laws (e.g., Darwinian gradualism), then the paleontologist's scientific mandate is to discover new laws of nature that can account for the recalcitrant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gould frames this as a consequence of viewing science as projecting laws to unobserved cases: unexplained fossil patterns are opportunities and, in a sense, a mandate to seek lawlike explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate laws from immanent processes rather than configurational events
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be 'based on immanent processes that produce events, not on the events themselves'—do not attempt to make laws out of contingent/configurational fossil outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Configurational properties (the particular historical states recorded in fossils) are low-probability, contingent outcomes; successful lawmaking must focus on underlying processes (mechanisms) that generate events so laws are genuinely nomic and general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from inductivist/observational mode to model construction and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Paleontology must move away from mere descriptive natural history and toward constructing models of evolutionary processes and using fossils to test those models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shift is needed because inductivism promotes searching for laws among configurational properties (which is unfruitful); models allow testing hypotheses about immanent processes and support nomothetic inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor idealized, interpretable models over purely descriptive fits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Idealized models are favored over actual specimens"; choose simple functional expressions with a minimum of non-interpretable parameters rather than highly parameterized fits that only describe particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate statistical fit matters, but simplicity, interpretability, and general applicability are also crucial. The power function y = b x^c is cited as valuable because it balances fit, simplicity, and interpretability even when more complex formulas can achieve closer fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model virtues: adequacy of fit, simplicity, interpretability, and generality
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' formula/model should provide adequate statistical fit across many cases, be reasonably simple, and have interpretable parameters that permit biological understanding and extension to other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overfitting by adding non-interpretable parameters; prioritize models that reveal mechanistic or biological underpinnings, enabling application across systems and fostering explanatory power rather than mere descriptive accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design models to reflect beliefs about how nature works and test by match to observations
rubrics_metrics.description: By designing a model that encodes hypotheses about natural processes, an adequate match between model and observations supports the inference that the model captures genuine understanding and can be extended to other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model success gives warrant to apply the model elsewhere; modeling is both explanatory and heuristic—used to discover nomic regularities grounded in mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative approaches and database analysis to uncover statistical patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop quantitative approaches to fossil databases to detect statistical patterns that may indicate real signals in the fossil record (e.g., rates changes around mass extinctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such quantitative work complements modeling and provides empirical fuel for formulating and testing process-based laws; it helps identify nonuniformity in tempo and mode that may warrant new theoretical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part requirement for disciplinary emergence: demand and proprietary perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergence of an autonomous discipline requires (1) identification of a set of problems whose solution is in high demand and (2) proprietary access to the perspective best suited to solving those problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of laws-oriented programs often traces to absence of one of these factors: either the problems are not of sufficient interest to outsiders, or the discipline lacks a genuinely proprietary methodological or evidential perspective.
